Every class, ranked

Draft Rankings

Every team’s draft, every year, best to worst — graded not on how many points the class piled up, but on how far it ran past what the waiver wire was giving away free that season, and then read against the eleven other rooms drafting alongside it.

How this works

Two numbers per row, and the honest limits of both.

  • Only points scored while he was actually on that team. A player taken, dropped a few weeks in, and gone on to have a monster year for someone else earns the drafting team nothing here — that swing is what Steals & Busts (above) already judges, on its own terms. This asks a narrower question: of what a manager’s own roster banked, how much came from men he drafted rather than men he picked up later?
  • Value is measured against the wire, not in raw points. Every pick is worth what he scored for the team that drew him minus what a freely available player at his position was scoring over the same stretch — the same replacement line Steals & Busts holds single picks to, prorated by the weeks that team actually held him. Kickers and defences are left out, exactly as they are from the boards above and for the same reason: nobody streams them and then argues about where they went in the draft. This matters more than it sounds. The old raw-points version of this board rewarded doing nothing: it ran at −0.41 against a manager’s roster moves, so the fastest route up it was to draft sixteen men and never touch the waiver wire again. Its all-time runner-up was a 5–9 team that made one move all season and carried two kickers and two defences from week one to week seventeen — 467 points of streaming positions — plus a backup quarterback worth 283 who started three times. Measured against replacement instead, roster moves stop mattering (+0.13) and the number tracks wins better than the old sum did (+0.43 against +0.29). Both figures are plain correlations across the 96 team-drafts from 2018 on.
  • The score is relative to that season, which is the only way eras compare. 2014–2020 paid zero points per reception and 2021+ pays half a point; 2014 went further still, scoring yardage in flat whole-number blocks (1 point per 25 passing yards, per 10 rushing or receiving) rather than the fractional rates every later season uses — reverse-engineered against known season totals, not guessed. Rank on raw figures and the rulebook does the sorting: the old board’s bottom twenty was seventeen-parts 2014–2017. So each class is scored against the others drafting in its own year instead. 100 is an average draft for its season, and every 15 points is one standard deviation — the row also says where the class finished among its own leaguemates. The raw figures are still printed beside it; they just aren’t what the board sorts on.
  • 2014–2017 sit on a coarser basis, and are marked as such on every row. Working out what the wire was paying needs to know who was on your bench in week nine, and this file has no week-by-week roster history before 2018. Those four seasons keep the whole-class totals computed for them out-of-band — real per-game box scores pulled straight from ESPN, scored under this league’s actual historic rules, then attributed to whichever team’s roster carried each player that week — with kickers and defences included and two-point conversions uncounted, since the stats source doesn’t carry them. Their scores are honest against their own season and are placed on the board on that footing; they are not the same measurement as 2018+, and the row says so. Two team-years are left off entirely rather than shown with a misleading number: 2014 and 2015 “Beasts of the Middle East” both have corrupted roster records at the source (confirmed independently, not a bug here) — one is simply empty, the other full of players who’d retired years before that season.

Wheeling and dealing

Trades

Every deal the league has made — both sides of it, what each haul was worth, and who came out ahead. In-season player trades and draft-day pick swaps both. How the scoring works is spelled out just below.

How trades are judged

One idea, one example. Thirty seconds.

  • Every side is scored in extra lineup points. Each week he held the players, take the best lineup his roster could field — then take it again without them. The gap is what the trade earned him that week. Add the weeks up and that’s his number.
    You trade for a WR2 you needed. Best lineup with him 128.4, without him 117.9.+10.5 that week
    You trade for a backup QB who never starts. With him 121.0, without him 121.0.+0.0
  • The haul is judged as a whole, not man by man. Two running backs fighting over the same FLEX spot are worth one upgrade, not two.
  • A verdict needs a real gap. Won and Lost only appear when one side clearly got more: at least 8 extra points, and a gap that’s big next to the size of the deal — 12% of the larger side. Ten points decides a twenty-point trade; on a three-hundred-point one it’s noise. Anything closer is a coin toss and gets no tag.
  • Injury cover gets no verdict. Where either manager was patching a hole he didn’t choose, the numbers stand but the deal is tagged Damage control instead — nobody is credited with beating a man who had no choice.
  • A traded pick is judged by the man taken with it. Pick swaps are read straight off the draft board and reach back to 2014.
  • Coverage: player trades need week-by-week rosters, so they run from 2018. 2017’s deals are rebuilt from starting lineups — they name the players but can’t price them.
  • Mind the yardstick. This is a different measure than Steals & Busts below: Steals & Busts asks how a player compared with the best free agent at his position. A trade asks something different — how much better your own lineup actually got. That’s deliberate: a trade is only worth what it changed for you.

Lineup decisions

Start & Sit

What every manager actually started, against the best lineup their roster could have produced that week. Points left on the bench are the difference. Covers 2018–2025, regular season and winner’s bracket only.

Decision record

Ranked by winnable losses — games lost where the best available lineup would have beaten the opponent’s score. The next column shows how many of those came in the winner’s bracket, and whether any cost the Alma Bowl. A perfect week means no lineup from that roster would have scored more. Managers with fewer than 30 weeks on file are marked — a short run is not a fair comparison.

The ones that hurt

Every winner’s-bracket loss a better lineup would have won, listed in full and ordered by what it cost — the title first, then a playoff exit. The heaviest benchings from everywhere else follow.

Perfect lineups

Weeks where nothing on the bench would have helped. Only counting weeks where the bench actually scored, so an empty bench doesn’t earn credit.

Hindsight

Steals & Busts

Who won and lost their season at the draft table and on the waiver wire.

How this works

One idea, one example. Thirty seconds.

  • Every number here is extra points. Not total points — points beyond what a free agent at the same position would have given you.
    Your TE scores 14.2. Best free TE scored 4.1.+10.1 extra
    Your QB scores 20.4. Best free QB scored 18.6.+1.8 extra
    Same twenty points on the scoreboard, wildly different weeks. Add up a season and that’s the number on the card.
  • Which free agent? In a normal week the twelve teams start about 12 QBs, 29 RBs, 31 WRs and 12 TEs. So line the running backs up by what they scored that week: the top 29 were in somebody’s lineup, and number 30 was not. He’s the one anybody could have had.
  • Left out: kickers, defenses and trades — trades are judged in their own section above, against a different yardstick. And a draft pick only counts as a steal if the manager kept the player — Adam drafted Justin Jefferson in 2020, cut him, then claimed him back in week 4, so that’s one of the best pickups on record rather than one of the best picks.

From the draft

Counted within his position, against the men drafted alongside him — a back taken twelfth of the fifty-seven RBs off the board who finishes third among them climbed nine spots. Both numbers come from that same fifty-seven, so the difference between them means something. Three names per position, so the board isn’t all quarterbacks.

From the waiver wire

A pickup gets credit for what he scored while you kept him. A drop gets charged with everything he scored for other teams after you let him go — and claiming him back stops the bleeding, because from then on he’s scoring for you again.

Extremes & oddities

Record Book

Drawn from the 1,000 games that count — every regular-season and winner’s-bracket game from 2014 to 2025. The consolation ladders settle placement, so they sit this out.

How the league changed

Rules

Every season’s settings, pulled from the league record. The starting lineup has never changed in twelve years — 1 QB, 2 RB, 2 WR, 1 TE, 1 FLEX, 1 D/ST, 1 K and a seven-man bench. Almost everything else has moved at least once, scoring included: in 2014 yardage paid whole points per block of yards, which is why every score that season is a round number.

What changed, and when

Values in full ink are the ones that changed that season; everything grayed carried over from the year before.

How points are scored

The current rulebook, taken from the league’s own scoring settings. Half a point per catch since 2021; before that, none.

Notes & Methodology

Source

The league's final standings, season stats and playoff pages, 2014–2025. Rank is final placement after the playoffs.

The Alma & The Emily

The championship game is the Alma Bowl, and its winner takes The Alma. The Emily Bowl settles last place, and its Emily Bowl Champion takes The Emily.

Format

Ten teams over 13 games in 2014–2015, twelve teams from 2016, and 14 games from 2021. Teams are grouped by the manager behind them, so a rebrand does not start a new franchise.

Records

Only Winner’s bracket games count toward playoff records and the record book; the consolation ladders settle placement only. A first-round bye is not counted as a playoff game. Regular-season win–loss, points, differential, moves and splits cover all twelve seasons; the 2014 and 2015 figures are rebuilt from the league’s own weekly scores and season records. Playoff win–loss covers the seasons with a bracket on file.

Seasons before 2018

ESPN keeps no bench for 2014–2017, but still holds the starting lineup and each starter’s points for every matchup period. A team-week is only shown where those starters reconcile to the score on the scoreboard — 524 of 696 do, and all but one of those to the point. The rest come back truncated and are left out. Because there is no bench, those seasons cannot feed Start & Sit or the waiver wire.

Opponents

Each line shows the club a player was on that week and who they faced, taken from nflverse’s schedule and weekly rosters. The league export stores only one club per player — the one he finished at — which was wrong for 1,732 of 20,996 player-weeks, so the club shown here is the one he actually played for. Where that can’t be established the row falls back to the export’s own code and no fixture is printed.

Player links

Every player name opens his game log for that season on Pro-Football-Reference, and a team defense opens that club’s schedule for the year. One line at the top of the script (LINK_TO) switches the whole page to ESPN instead. The league export carries no external id, so the ids were matched in from nflverse’s public player table and pinned down by position and by the seasons each man was actually rostered here — which is what separates one Steve Smith from another. All 1,361 names in the archive resolve, on both sites.
